title: Fixed-parameter tractability of graph isomorphism by rank-width
formal: Do a computable function \(f:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\), an absolute constant c and a deterministic algorithm exist which decide isomorphism of graphs G,H in time \(f(k)(|V(G)|+|V(H)|+2)^{c}\), where \(k=\max (\operatorname{rw}(G),\operatorname{rw}(H))\)?
definitions: Graphs are finite simple undirected graphs given by adjacency matrices. Isomorphism is a vertex bijection preserving adjacency. For a graph G and \(X\subseteq V(G)\), the cut-rank is the rank over the two-element field of the adjacency submatrix with rows X and columns \(V(G)\setminus X\). A rank decomposition is a tree of maximum degree three whose leaves are bijectively labeled by \(V(G)\). Every tree edge partitions the leaves and hence defines a cut-rank; the decomposition width is the maximum of those ranks. Rank-width \(\operatorname{rw}(G)\) is the minimum width, with \(\operatorname{rw}(G)=0\) for at most one vertex. No decomposition or parameter value is supplied to the algorithm. The exponent c is independent of the rank-width.

context_blocks.text: Rank-width measures graph complexity through low-rank adjacency cuts and supports many structural algorithms. Graph isomorphism on bounded rank-width is tractable at each fixed width, but that does not by itself yield one exponent independent of the parameter.

Neuen’s 2026 survey identifies the remaining parameterized isomorphism frontiers. An \(n^{g(k)}\) algorithm or a quasipolynomial dependence involving n does not establish fixed-parameter tractability. The target concerns testing isomorphism, without additionally demanding canonization.

why: Resolve a major parameterized isomorphism boundary for a broad graph-decomposition measure.
